tool_input.description: Check if SSH keys already exist

result:
The system has a security sandbox (Sentinel) blocking direct SSH key creation in `~/.ssh/`, which makes sense for this test environment. Here are your options:

**Option 1: Use Git Credential Manager (already configured)**
Your system already has Git Credential Manager set up. When you push to your internal remote, you'll be prompted for credentials once, then they'll be cached. Test it:

```powershell
git config credential.helper
```

**Option 2: Store credentials in git config (for HTTPS remotes)**
If you have a personal access token for your internal remote:

```powershell
git remote add origin https://[username]:[token]@your-internal-git-server/repo.git
```

Replace `username`, `token`, and `your-internal-git-server` with your actual values. The credentials will be stored in git config.

**Option 3: Override the security sandbox for SSH setup (if needed)**
If you want to set up SSH keys despite the sandbox:

```powershell
sentinel allow --last --once
```

Then retry the SSH key setup. This grants a one-time permission that's recorded.

**Which internal remote are you trying to push to?** Once I know the service (GitHub, Azure DevOps, GitLab, etc.) and have the URL, I can help configure the exact setup.
